name: French
region: France, Belgium, Switzerland, Canada and much of West and Central Africa
about: French is an official language on five continents and a working language of the United Nations, the Olympics and many international bodies. About a third of English vocabulary comes from French, so you already know more words than you think.
pronunciation: Final consonants are usually silent, so petit sounds like puh-tee and Paris sounds like pa-ree.
The French R is made at the back of the throat, a little like a soft gargle, not rolled like the Hindi R.
Nasal vowels in words like bon and vin are said through the nose without fully pronouncing the N.
The letter U is said with rounded lips while saying ee, a sound between ee and oo.

lessons.intro: Bonjour! Let's start with the words you'll use every single day in France. French people greet each other a lot, so these will take you far.
lessons.tip: Always say bonjour when you walk into a shop, café or lift. Skipping it is considered rude, and a friendly bonjour gets you much better service.

phrases.note: Bonjour literally means good day. Use it with anyone until early evening. With friends you can say salut, which is casual.
Comment allez-vous is the polite way to ask how someone is. With friends, simply say ça va, which means how's it going.
Je vais bien, merci means I am well, thank you. In casual chat, people just say ça va, the same words used to ask the question.
Merci means thank you and works everywhere. Add beaucoup to say merci beaucoup, which means thank you very much.
Excusez-moi is polite for excuse me, to get attention. Pardon is a quick sorry when you bump into someone. For a real apology, say je suis désolée.
Au revoir is the standard goodbye and means until we see again. À bientôt means see you soon. Friends often just say salut or ciao.

lessons.intro: Now let's introduce ourselves. A few simple sentences will help you make friends in France, whether at university, at work or on holiday.
lessons.tip: French has two words for you. Use vous with strangers, elders and at work, and tu with friends and children. Wait for the other person to suggest tu.

phrases.note: Je m'appelle Priya literally means I call myself Priya. It is the most natural way to say your name in French.
Comment vous appelez-vous is the polite way to ask someone's name. With a friend or a young person, say comment tu t'appelles.
Vous venez d'où means where do you come from. It is polite yet natural. With friends, say tu viens d'où.
Je viens d'Inde means I come from India. You can also say je suis indienne, meaning I am Indian. A man would say indien.
Enchantée means delighted to meet you. It is spelled with an extra E when a woman says it, but sounds the same when a man says enchanté.
Je parle un peu français means I speak a little French. People will often slow down and be very encouraging when they hear it.

lessons.intro: Time for numbers! Counting in French is fun, and you'll need it for prices, phone numbers and train times.
lessons.tip: In France, times are often given on the twenty-four hour clock, especially for trains and shops. So quinze heures means three in the afternoon.

phrases.note: Un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq. These are one to five. Un becomes une before feminine words, as in une heure, one hour.
Six, sept, huit, neuf, dix. These are six to ten. Notice the P in sept is silent, and the H in huit is silent too.
Quelle heure est-il is the standard way to ask the time. In everyday speech you will also hear il est quelle heure.
Aujourd'hui means today. It is one long word, so say it smoothly, oh zhoor dwee.
Demain means tomorrow. A handy phrase is à demain, which means see you tomorrow.
Hier means yesterday. The H is silent, so it sounds like ee-yair.

lessons.intro: France is famous for its food, so let's learn to order, ask prices and pay. Bon appétit is just around the corner!
lessons.tip: In restaurants, the waiter will not bring the bill until you ask for it, because rushing guests is seen as rude. Service is already included, so tipping is optional.

phrases.note: C'est combien means how much is it. A slightly more formal version is combien ça coûte, meaning how much does it cost.
C'est trop cher means it is too expensive. Bargaining is rare in French shops, but you can use this at flea markets.
De l'eau, s'il vous plaît means some water, please. Ask for une carafe d'eau to get free tap water in a restaurant.
Je suis végétarienne means I am vegetarian, said by a woman. A man says végétarien. It helps to add pas de viande, meaning no meat.
C'est délicieux means it is delicious. The chef will be happy to hear it. Casually, you can also say c'est très bon.
L'addition, s'il vous plaît means the bill, please. Catch the waiter's eye and say it politely.

lessons.intro: Let's get moving! These phrases will help you find your way around French cities, from the metro to the train station.
lessons.tip: Before asking a stranger for directions, always start with excusez-moi, madame or excusez-moi, monsieur. It makes the request sound polite and friendly.

phrases.note: Où est la gare means where is the train station. Big cities have several stations, like la gare de Lyon in Paris.
Tournez à gauche means turn left. You will hear this form from people giving you polite directions.
Tournez à droite means turn right. Be careful not to mix it up with tout droit, which means straight ahead.
Allez tout droit means go straight ahead. Listen carefully, because tout droit sounds close to à droite.
C'est loin means is it far. To ask the exact distance, say c'est à quelle distance.

phrases.roman: poo-vay voo may-day, seel voo play
phrases.note: Pouvez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît means can you help me, please. In an emergency, simply shout au secours.

lessons.intro: Last lesson! These little phrases keep any conversation going, even when you don't understand everything. Let's finish strong.
lessons.tip: French people often say d'accord to mean okay or agreed, and bon to fill pauses. Using them makes your French sound instantly more natural.

phrases.note: Oui means yes and non means no. If someone asks a negative question and you want to say yes, use si instead.
Je ne comprends pas means I don't understand. In casual speech people drop the ne and say je comprends pas.

phrases.native: Parlez plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
phrases.roman: par-lay plew lahnt-mahn, seel voo play
phrases.note: Parlez plus lentement, s'il vous plaît means please speak more slowly. It is polite and people will gladly do it.
Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire means what does that mean. Literally, it is what does that want to say.
Ça me plaît means I like it, literally it pleases me. You can also say j'aime bien, which is equally common.
Bonne nuit means good night, said before going to bed. When leaving someone in the evening, say bonsoir or bonne soirée instead.
